State World Models: Execute the Rules, Generate the Pixels

Chan Yan Ki     Yanran Zhang     Wenzhao Zheng     Xiaofeng Wang Affiliation:  Department of Automation, Tsinghua University, China        Zheng Zhu     Lei Chen     Jie Zhou     Jiwen Lu Affiliation:  Department of Automation, Tsinghua University, China     Affiliation:  GigaAI Project Page  |   GitHub  |   Hugging Face  |   ModelScope
Abstract

Existing world models can generate action-conditioned video from a single image. Many focus on camera movement, allowing users to explore the generated scene. However, navigation alone does not ensure that an action follows persistent rules when its outcome depends on state that is invisible in the current frame. We present Stateful Harness, a framework that separates world evolution from video rendering to support stateful and rule-governed interaction. It maintains an evolving world state under specified rules, renders each resulting event with a frozen video model, and uses the generated clip to update the world state for the next turn. At each turn, the harness resolves the action selected by the user and compiles the resulting event into an instruction, while a preview clip from an editable 3D scene provides spatial and camera guidance. To evaluate rule compliance, we build WorldState-Bench, a benchmark of 50 counterfactual twin pairs that share an initial frame and action but differ in hidden state and required outcome. Under rule-only prompting, the best of the 11 evaluated video backends produces the required endings for both cases in 32% of pairs. For MiniMax-H3, specifying the required endings raises this rate from 32% to 64%, while the full harness reaches 92% with the same frozen model. These results support separating rule execution from video rendering for world interactions with hidden state.

1 Introduction

Video generation has advanced rapidly, with recent models producing visually realistic videos with coherent motion (Wan et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2025). Building on this progress, interactive video world models condition generation on navigation signals, allowing users to move through and explore generated environments (Parker-Holder and Fruchter, 2025; Wang et al., 2026).

Navigation control makes a generated scene explorable, but does not determine the consequences of interacting with it (Parker-Holder and Fruchter, 2025; Wang et al., 2026). Some video world models support richer interactions by conditioning generation on player or agent actions (Valevski et al., 2025; Zhu et al., 2026a). However, a responsive video does not by itself ensure that an action has the outcome required by the world state and rules, or that its consequences persist across later interactions (Ding et al., 2026; Xu et al., 2026a). For example, the same action should open a locked chest only when the player holds a key, even if the initial views are identical (Figure 2). Such distinctions require semantic state to record variables such as inventory and progress, together with an addressable spatial state to preserve scene layout and camera paths across turns. While prior systems incorporate explicit state through programmable engines, learned game variables, or reconstructed NPC state (Huang et al., 2026; Lin et al., 2026; Deng et al., 2026), their evaluations focus on selected mechanics and do not establish whether a frozen video model can render outcomes prescribed by newly specified rules involving hidden state. Explicit state alone does not ensure that the consequence required by its rules appears in the generated video. The central challenge is therefore to make state transitions authoritative and render their consequences faithfully.

We present Stateful Harness, a framework that separates world evolution from video rendering to support stateful interaction under specified rules (Figure 1). It maintains an evolving world state under specified rules, renders each resulting event with a frozen video model, and uses the generated clip to update the world state for the next turn. Given a world description and an initial image, a coding agent defines the world state, available actions, and executable rules, while an editable 3D scene represents the spatial layout. The rules remain fixed as the world state evolves through user actions. At each turn, the user observes the current scene and selects an action, which the runtime resolves against the current state before rendering. The resolved event is compiled into a VisualScript instruction, and a preview clip from the updated 3D scene provides spatial and camera guidance. A frozen video model renders the event from these inputs and a visual anchor drawn from the initial image or preceding clip. A vision language model then interprets the generated clip and proposes updates to the semantic and spatial state based on the observed events. The runtime incorporates updates compatible with the fixed rules, and the resulting state determines the consequences of subsequent actions. Together, rule execution, video generation, and visual observation form a closed loop that yields state world models.

To evaluate whether an action yields a visible event consistent with hidden state, we construct WorldState-Bench with a Change-to-Comply protocol. Change assesses whether the action produces a discernible event, and Comply assesses whether that event satisfies an executable rule. Each of the 50 cases comprises a counterfactual pair with the same initial frame, action, and rule program but different hidden values that require distinct outcomes. We introduce PairFollow and PairStrict as two metrics for joint evaluation of each counterfactual pair. PairFollow requires both clips to show their required endings, whereas PairStrict additionally requires the forbidden ending to be absent from both clips. Among eleven unwrapped video backends, the highest PairFollow score under the Rule-only condition is 32%. For MiniMax-H3, explicitly specifying the required ending increases PairFollow from 32% to 64%, although PairStrict reaches only 4%. With MiniMax-H3, the complete Stateful Harness framework achieves 92% PairFollow and 90% PairStrict on the same cases. Beyond the single-turn probe, the same closed loop carries state across longer episodes, as in the multi-turn duel of Figure 6, and extends training-free to worlds whose custom rules and state are written as a new world definition.

2 Related Work

World Models. World models study action-conditioned predictions (Micheli et al., 2022; Hafner et al., 2025; Ha and Schmidhuber, 2018). The Genie series introduces latent actions and promptable environments (Bruce et al., 2024; Parker-Holder et al., 2024; Parker-Holder and Fruchter, 2025), while Oasis demonstrates interaction in an open world (Decart and Etched, 2024). Other systems expand scene range, streaming, and instruction following (He et al., 2025b; Wang et al., 2026; Robbyant Team et al., 2026; Yin et al., 2026; DreamX Team et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2026a), separate appearance from actions (Yu et al., 2025b), use game corpora (Che et al., 2025; Kanervisto et al., 2025; Guo et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2024a; Tang et al., 2025), or address memory and visual consistency (Xiao et al., 2025; Yu et al., 2025a; Li et al., 2025b; Hu et al., 2026; Garcin et al., 2026). Building on action-conditioned rendering, Stateful Harness uses executable rules to resolve each action against explicit semantic and spatial state before a frozen video model renders the resulting event.

Geometric Control of Video Generation. Camera-conditioned systems inject trajectories through learned pose or motion representations (Wang et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2024b; He et al., 2025a; Xu et al., 2024; Bahmani et al., 2025). Other methods reconstruct geometry for training-free control (Hou and Chen, 2024) or use boxes, source videos, and reference clips (Lin et al., 2023; Bai et al., 2025; Jiang et al., 2025). MoGe4D generates trajectories over recovered geometry (Zhang et al., 2026b). The Stateful Harness uses a related interface to carry an editable scene across turns, with rule execution determining which spatial edits and semantic events are sent to the renderer.

Explicit State and Rules. Rules can be searched as generative objects or compiled from language (Salen and Zimmerman, 2003; Cook et al., 2013; Hsu et al., 2026). PWM couples an engine and a 3D oriented-box representation with conditioning at the pixel level (Huang et al., 2026). Code World Model compiles a code-maintained state into proxy video and fine-tunes its renderer (Chen et al., 2026b). Other work generates rule code without a video renderer (Lehrach et al., 2026), recovers state from generated frames (Deng et al., 2026), or conditions generation on selected state variables (Lin et al., 2026; Meng et al., 2026; Zhu et al., 2026a). Narrative and character state can also be generated together (Li et al., 2025a; Cheng et al., 2025). We combine a persistent editable scene, a semantic state ledger, and the standard reference inputs of a frozen renderer. This combination is minimal: new rule-governed worlds reduce to a small typed program, no engine or fine-tuning. Table 12 compares these interfaces and evaluation protocols.

World Modeling Evaluation. Most existing benchmarks measure visual quality, prompt adherence, navigation, subject actions, event editing, and perspective changes (Ying et al., 2026; Xu et al., 2026b; Xu et al., 2026a; Zhao et al., 2026; Ding et al., 2026; Fang et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2026). Camera and geometry states can be tracked or remembered (Nam et al., 2026; Yu et al., 2025a; Li et al., 2025b). These measurements are valuable for navigability and continuity, but they do not directly test whether identical images and actions produce different rule-mandated outcomes when only hidden state changes. Concurrent work tests whether a shell-game arrangement is retained in the model’s internal state across a swap chain (Shin et al., 2026). WorldState-Bench instead keeps the hidden state in an explicit rule program and tests whether the mandated outcome is executed in rendered video. Benchmarks inside executable games can compare behavior with engine state (Hafner, 2022; Bard et al., 2020; Light et al., 2023; Ouyang et al., 2026; La et al., 2026; Luo et al., 2026), but require an existing game or simulator. WorldState-Bench supplies an explicit rule program and tests its consequences in generated video.

3 Method: The Stateful Harness

Framework Overview. A video model can depict an interaction, but a generated clip alone does not specify which changes should persist or whether those changes satisfy the rules of the world. Figure 2 shows how identical frames and actions require different outcomes when the hidden state differs. Inspired by the role of LLM harnesses, we place a stateful runtime around a frozen video model to separate rule execution, visual realization, and observation of the generated result.

Given a world description and an initial image, a coding agent constructs an executable game definition containing the state schema, available actions, rules, events, goals, and visual semantics. The harness initializes a semantic ledger and an editable 3D scene, while the game definition remains fixed throughout the episode. At each turn, the user observes the current scene and selects an action, which the runtime resolves against the current state and rules to determine the event and provisional state. The resolved event is compiled into a VisualScript instruction, and a preview clip from the updated 3D scene provides spatial and camera guidance. A frozen video model generates the next clip from these inputs and a visual anchor drawn from the initial image or preceding clip. A vision language model then interprets the generated events and proposes updates to the semantic and spatial state. The runtime checks these proposals against the fixed rules and incorporates compatible updates into the world state used to resolve the next action. The final frame also becomes the visual anchor for the next generation step. Together, rule execution, video generation, and visual observation form a closed loop that couples explicit world state with a frozen video model, yielding a state world model. Figure 3 illustrates world construction and the rule to render path.

We represent the evolving world state as st=(zt,ut)∈𝒮sem×𝒮sps_{t}=(z_{t},u_{t})\in\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{sem}}\times\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{sp}}. The semantic component ztz_{t} records resources, entity attributes, progress, attitudes, and terminal status that may be invisible in the current frame. The spatial component utu_{t} records an editable entity layout, scale, and camera path. A fixed rule program RR determines which events an action permits and which state changes those events require. The harness updates the world state through a closed loop,

st+1=ℋR​(st,at,ot+1).s_{t+1}=\mathcal{H}_{R}(s_{t},\,a_{t},\,o_{t+1}). (1)

Here ot+1o_{t+1} denotes observations extracted by a vision language model from the generated clip, and ℋR\mathcal{H}_{R} combines rule execution with compatible updates derived from these observations. The next state therefore incorporates both the consequences of the action and feedback from the generated video under the fixed rules RR. The visual anchor ftf_{t} is initialized from the supplied image and subsequently updated from the final frame of each clip.

3.1 Stage 0: World Construction

World construction produces an executable game definition, an initial frame, a semantic ledger, and an editable spatial scene. The game definition fixes the rules for an episode, whereas the ledger and scene change as interactions unfold.

Executable Rules. From the world description, a coding agent writes the game definition in a small typed language. Each rule has a guard that reads the current state and action, and an effect that specifies ledger updates, spatial edits, and an event. Goal conditions inspect the ledger to determine whether an episode has ended. The agent validates and freezes the definition before interaction begins. In the counterfactual benchmark, both members of a pair share this definition.

Initial Frame and Spatial State. The benchmark supplies an audited first image shared by each counterfactual pair. For a new world, setup accepts a supplied image. A feed forward geometry model lifts the image into instance boxes and initializes u0u_{0} as an untextured, editable 3D scene with a ground plane and labeled cuboids. We call this scene the clay model. Its explicit geometry supports object edits and procedural camera previews across turns.

Semantic State. The ledger is a serializable record of typed fields for resources, entity attributes, progress counters, attitudes, and terminal status. A twin specification declares the theme, twin identifier, and seeds. The initializer assigns different hidden values zA≠zBz_{A}\neq z_{B} while preserving the same first frame and spatial layout. The rules therefore require different outcomes for the same visible action, even though rendering remains stochastic.

3.2 Stage 1: State Evolution and Video Generation

A turn begins when the user selects an action ata_{t} after observing the current scene. In open interaction an intent agent can map a user instruction to a structured action. The runtime first settles the rule governed outcome, then compiles and renders it, and finally observes the generated clip for changes relevant to the next turn. This order gives fixed rules authority over action consequences while allowing generated events to inform the evolving world state.

Rule Settlement. The rule program evaluates its guards against sts_{t} and ata_{t} before video generation. It produces a provisional semantic state z¯t+1\bar{z}_{t+1}, a rule event ete_{t}, and a spatial edit script ϵt\epsilon_{t}. The edit script may add, move, or remove a box or change the camera path. The provisional spatial state is obtained by applying these edits to the clay model.

(z¯t+1,ϵt,et)=τR​(st,at),u¯t+1=apply⁡(ut,ϵt),s¯t+1=(z¯t+1,u¯t+1).(\bar{z}_{t+1},\,\epsilon_{t},\,e_{t})\;=\;\tau_{R}(s_{t},\,a_{t}),\qquad\bar{u}_{t+1}\;=\;\mathrm{apply}(u_{t},\,\epsilon_{t}),\qquad\bar{s}_{t+1}\;=\;(\bar{z}_{t+1},\,\bar{u}_{t+1}). (2)

An optional neural kernel ρ\rho may propose dialogue or freeform narration for the settled event. Schema validation, value clamping, bounded retry, and fallback to the rule defined default constrain its proposals to the allowed set 𝒜τ​(s,a)\mathcal{A}_{\tau}(s,a). Thus the gated kernel 𝒢∘ρ\mathcal{G}\circ\rho satisfies

Supp((𝒢∘ρ)(⋅∣s,a))⊆𝒜τ(s,a).\mathrm{Supp}\big((\mathcal{G}\circ\rho)(\cdot\mid s,a)\big)\;\subseteq\;\mathcal{A}_{\tau}(s,a). (3)

The proposal may vary how an allowed event is expressed but cannot change the rule mandated transition in Eq. 2.

Spatial Guidance. The runtime applies ϵt\epsilon_{t} to the clay model before rendering so that the preview represents the provisional spatial state. A procedural camera program renders this into a preview clip rtr_{t}, which is an editable representation of layout and cameras rather than the final appearance.

Instruction Compilation. The VisualScript compiler translates the settled state and event into a typed visual script with slots for actor, action, target, reaction, dialogue, effects, end state, and shots. A fixed compiler maps this record to the text instruction ptp_{t}, so identical inputs produce identical instructions. The text carries semantic facts that an oriented box stream cannot express, while the preview supplies layout and camera guidance. The instruction identifies the preview as a spatial reference to discourage the backend from reproducing its clay appearance.

Frozen Video Rendering. The video model receives the instruction as text, the preview clip as video reference, and the visual anchor ftf_{t} as image reference. It generates a clip vt+1v_{t+1} depicting the settled event, and the last frame becomes the anchor for the next turn.

(pt,rt)=𝒞⁡(z¯t+1,u¯t+1,et),vt+1=Vθ​(pt,rt,ft),ft+1=last⁡(vt+1).(p_{t},\,r_{t})\;=\;\mathcal{C}(\bar{z}_{t+1},\,\bar{u}_{t+1},\,e_{t}),\qquad v_{t+1}\;=\;V_{\theta}(p_{t},\,r_{t},\,f_{t}),\qquad f_{t+1}\;=\;\mathrm{last}(v_{t+1}). (4)

The model weights remain frozen, and the runtime uses the stock text, image, and video reference interfaces of a compatible backend. Normal operation makes one generation request per turn, with bounded retries for transient errors. On a scene change, the anchor chain can be reset and appearance information is carried in the instruction instead.

Visual Observation and State Update. A vision language model examines the generated clip together with the settled event and provisional state. It identifies visible events and proposes changes to semantic or spatial fields that the video makes observable. The runtime admits a proposed change only when it is well formed and compatible with the fixed rule program. A visual detail may therefore become part of the next state, while an apparent event that contradicts the settled outcome is recorded as a rendering inconsistency and cannot overturn that outcome. We express this step as

ot+1=Oψ​(vt+1,s¯t+1,et),st+1=UR​(s¯t+1,ot+1),o_{t+1}\;=\;O_{\psi}(v_{t+1},\,\bar{s}_{t+1},\,e_{t}),\qquad s_{t+1}\;=\;U_{R}(\bar{s}_{t+1},\,o_{t+1}), (5)

where OψO_{\psi} proposes observations and URU_{R} validates and incorporates permitted updates. The next action is evaluated against st+1s_{t+1}, closing the interaction loop without changing the rules RR. The counterfactual evaluation in this paper tests rendered compliance.

4 Benchmark: WorldState-Bench

Overview. Existing benchmarks evaluate visual quality, prompt adherence, navigation, subject actions, event editing, and camera or geometric consistency (Ying et al., 2026; Xu et al., 2026b; Xu et al., 2026a; Zhao et al., 2026; Ding et al., 2026; Fang et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2026; Nam et al., 2026). These evaluations do not directly isolate whether a change in hidden state produces the distinct visible consequence prescribed by an executable rule. Benchmarks based on executable games assess behavior conditioned on state provided by existing engines (Hafner, 2022; Bard et al., 2020; Light et al., 2023; Ouyang et al., 2026; La et al., 2026; Luo et al., 2026). Worlds initialized from a description and an image lack this predefined engine state. To evaluate such worlds, WorldState-Bench uses counterfactual pairs with identical visible inputs, different hidden values, and expected outcomes determined by an executable rule before generation. Joint evaluation of each pair tests whether both required outcomes are rendered correctly under the corresponding hidden states.

We formalize this with the Change-to-Comply protocol. Change assesses whether an action produces a discernible event beyond camera motion. Comply assesses whether the event satisfies the rule for the specified hidden state. This separates the absence of an event from the generation of an event that contradicts the rule. The primary metrics quantify Comply, while clips with no discernible event or unjudgeable content are recorded as Unclear and receive no credit.

Counterfactual Hidden-State Pairs. Each case contains two counterfactual instances, A and B, that share the same first frame and action script. They differ in one hidden value zA≠zBz_{A}\neq z_{B} that is not observable in the shared frame. The same rule program requires different visible endings for the two instances. A correct ending in an isolated clip does not establish sensitivity to hidden state, whereas identical endings across a pair necessarily violate the required outcome for at least one instance. We therefore count a pair as compliant only when both clips show their required endings. A stricter criterion additionally requires the forbidden ending to be absent throughout both clips.

Case Construction. The benchmark comprises 50 cases drawn from 49 hidden variables and 21 scenario themes. Hidden values select which object, character, or elemental form carries the effect. Each hidden variable must be unobservable in the first frame and must select rule branches with visibly different outcomes. FLUX.2 (Black Forest Labs, 2025) generates the shared first frame at 1280×7201280{\times}720, and each frame is audited for visual cues that reveal the hidden value. This audit forms part of benchmark construction. Authors specify each case program in a typed language that determines the initial states, required endings, and fixed choice judging questions. The harness executes the same rules used to derive the expected outcomes, so the evaluation measures whether the generated videos depict these outcomes.

We compile two instruction conditions from each case specification. Rule-only provides the original case instruction, hidden value, selected rule branch, and action. Rule+end additionally specifies the required terminal outcome in an explicit final state sentence. Table 1 reports results under these conditions, while the harness uses the VisualScript instruction described in §3.2.

Judging. We use the multimodal Qwen3.8-27B-VL (Yang and others, 2025) to answer fixed choice questions from sampled video frames. The questions identify the ending shown and determine whether the forbidden outcome appears at any point in the clip. At the clip level, EndFollow requires the prescribed ending, CntAbsent requires the absence of the forbidden outcome, and Strict requires both conditions. At the pair level, PairFollow and PairStrict require both clips to satisfy EndFollow and Strict, respectively. TwinContrast records whether the judged endings differ between the two clips. The judge receives the expected outcomes for the relevant rule branch, but neither the hidden variable nor the rule text.

5 Experiments

5.1 Experiment Setup

The rule compliance experiments use the 50 counterfactual pairs in WorldState-Bench, with 100 clips for individual evaluation and 50 pairs for joint evaluation (§4). Each backend generates one clip of a few seconds per action at its native resolution and frame rate. Clips contain 77 to 128 frames at 15 to 24 fps, with resolutions from 592×336592{\times}336 to 1280×7201280{\times}720. The harness generates clips at 864×480864{\times}480 and 24 fps. We evaluate eleven existing backends without additional training or fine-tuning (Table 1). Four image-to-video generators receive instruction text and the initial frame, namely Wan2.2 (Wan et al., 2025), LongCat-Video (LongCat Team et al., 2025), HunyuanVideo 1.5 (Wu et al., 2025), and MiniMax-H3 (Chen et al., 2026a). Seven interactive world models receive inputs through their standard action interfaces, namely LingBot-World v2 (Robbyant Team et al., 2026), Echo-WM Flash (Zhang et al., 2026a), FantasyWorld (Dai et al., 2026), AlayaWorld (AlayaWorld Team et al., 2026), InSpatio-World (InSpatio Team et al., 2026), Astra (Zhu et al., 2026b), and HY-WorldPlay (Sun et al., 2025). The Qwen3.8-27B-VL judge evaluates frames sampled at 3 fps together with the final frame. Generation and judging use eight A800 80 GB GPUs.

5.2 Results on WorldState-Bench

Under Rule-only prompting, MiniMax-H3 achieves 66% EndFollow and 32% PairFollow, while Wan2.2 achieves 65% and 32%, respectively (Table 1). The lower joint accuracy indicates that correct outcomes in individual clips do not imply compliance across both hidden states. Astra, HY-WorldPlay, and InSpatio-World achieve less than 20% EndFollow despite high CntAbsent scores. These results indicate that the absence of forbidden content can coincide with failure to generate the required event. Explicit outcome instructions under the Rule+end probe (Track B) improve EndFollow for several backends but do not establish reliable joint compliance. The highest unwrapped PairStrict score is 26% for Wan2.2, while MiniMax-H3 reaches only 4% PairStrict and 30% CntAbsent. The reported harness condition resolves each action before generation and does not use compliance judgments to select among repeated video samples.

With the same frozen MiniMax-H3 weights, the harness reaches 92% PairFollow, 90% PairStrict, and 96% TwinContrast (Table 1). In the blind human comparison, Stateful Harness is preferred in 98% of pairwise comparisons against four widely-used unwrapped baselines, with no comparison won by a baseline (Figure 5, Appendix C).

A component-chain decomposition on WorldState-Bench attributes the gain to outcome specification (+32 points) and to executed state with compiled references (+28 points), with both increments significant under paired exact McNemar tests over the 50 pairs.

5.3 Qualitative Results

Figure 4 shows counterfactual pairs in which unwrapped baselines include the forbidden outcome or reproduce an ending across both hidden states. Appendix Figures 13 and 14 show more pairs. The harness generates the distinct outcomes specified by the rules. Figure 6 illustrates how settled state changes condition subsequent generation, using three real harness episodes read through their HUDs. The three episodes span 15, 29, and 11 turns respectively, showing that Stateful Harness sustains multi-turn interaction on the same frozen weights. The episodes are also three genres: town exploration, dating narrative, and turn-based duel, each with its own state transitions and rules. Each genre is a new executable game definition on the same runtime and video model, instantiated training-free. Appendix Figures 15, 16, and 17 unroll all turns of the three episodes.

5.4 Additional Experiments

External Benchmark. Table 2 compares the twenty models reported by Ying et al. (2026) and their class averages with two configurations using frozen MiniMax-H3 weights. These configurations use the official text protocol and the full harness with the spatial preview video, respectively. Video quality (78.0) and physical plausibility (68.8) are close to the corresponding class averages for text-driven models (77.4 and 66.9). Setting adherence increases from 71.1 under the official protocol to 87.2, and the interaction score of 77.7 is the highest reported in the comparison.

Channel Ablation. Table 8 compares reference channel configurations while holding the video model weights fixed. First-frame anchoring raises the full split from 74.2 to 76.1 and setting adherence from 71.1 to 89.6, and adding the control video reaches 79.0 on navigation with interaction rising from 69.0 to 77.7, consistent with the preview’s camera guidance. Consistency dips from 83.8 to 75.3 and recovers to 77.8. Supplying the same control video under the raw text protocol yields 67.1 on the full split, improving camera trajectory scores. This transfer of the preview’s geometry and appearance into the output motivates instructions that specify how the reference should be interpreted. Thirty generated clips illustrate this effect: clay appearance arises when the instruction does not identify the reference as a layout preview (§3.2). On our benchmark, the same frozen weights under the full harness improve every metric in Table 1 over the raw baseline of its track by 30 to 86 points: EndFollow from 66 to 96, PairFollow from 32 to 92, TwinContrast from 32 to 96, and PairStrict from 4 to 90.

6 Conclusion

Navigation control enables exploration of a generated scene. Counterfactual pairs test whether the same action produces the distinct outcomes required by different hidden states under shared rules. On WorldState-Bench, unwrapped image-to-video backends often fail this test even when the ending is specified in the prompt. The Stateful Harness separates rule execution from video rendering, with explicit semantic and spatial state determining the event depicted by a frozen video model. Visual observations of the generated clip inform the state used in subsequent interactions. With MiniMax-H3 weights held fixed, PairFollow increases from 32% under Rule-only instructions and 64% with explicit ending instructions to 92% with the full harness. These results support explicit state and executable rules for controlling stateful rendered interactions. The same recipe already sustains multi-turn episodes of 11 to 29 turns and extends to spatial triggers, where the rule program, not the renderer, absorbs the added bookkeeping.

AI Usage Statement

We used generative AI tools for manuscript writing assistance and for auxiliary tooling scripts, but not for research ideation, experiment design, or producing any reported result. AI models are also used as system components, for judging generated videos and for constructing game definitions. All AI-assisted output was reviewed by authors, who take full responsibility for the final content.

Appendix

Appendix A WorldState-Bench: Case Construction Details

Case Anatomy.

Each case comprises five components. These components are a theme and scene description, a first frame generated by FLUX.2 at 1280×7201280{\times}720, a hidden variable declaration name∈{vA,vB}\texttt{name}\in\{v_{A},v_{B}\}, an action script, and rule text specifying distinct endings. Twins A/B share the theme, frame, action, and rules. They differ in the hidden value. The suite spans 21 themes (magic academy, dungeon, open-world exploration, dating, visual novel, museum, survival, escape room, sailing, farming, ranch, camping, shopkeeping, card games, board games, detective, turn-based combat, stealth, healing, cooking, and fishing) and 49 distinct hidden variables.

Hidden-Variable Families.

The hidden values fall into three response types. Mechanism selection decides which object or mechanism responds (42 cases, e.g., a gate mode that raises the stone door versus a brazier mode that lights tall flames). Character response decides whether a character or creature responds instead of an object (6 cases, e.g., sheep gathering at a trough, an NPC sitting down). Form selection decides which elemental form or scene side carries the effect (2 cases, e.g., red versus blue flames, the left versus the right brazier). All are invisible in the frame by construction and by audit.

Trigger Types.

Cases also differ in how the rule trigger is expressed, with cast covering verbal or ritual actions (20 clips), gesture covering physical actions (42), mechanism covering object interactions (26), and zone covering entry into or use of a spatial region (12). Zone-triggered cases are the most demanding (§5.2) because compliance additionally requires the render to make the zone’s state visible. This motivates the spatial channel.

Instruction Probes.

Every case is evaluated under two probes compiled from the same card. Rule-only provides the original “Inputs to the video model” text from the case specification, including the scene, shared action script, rule with both branches, and the consequence of the selected branch. Rule+end appends the required terminal state using the visual vocabulary defined for the case and explicitly asks the model to maintain this final state. The difference between the two conditions measures the effect of adding an explicit terminal outcome instruction. Table 5 reports this difference for each backend.

First-Frame Audit.

Each first frame undergoes eight rounds of VLM auditing across six dimensions to check for visible evidence of the hidden value. The dimensions are object presence, color attribution, text, spatial cues, count cues, and state cues. If the audit detects evidence of the hidden value, the frame is regenerated using a revised prompt. The audit prompts, model settings, and the regeneration log are part of the reproduction artifacts listed in Appendix H.

Rule Text.

Rules are written in plain English with fixed sentence frames per family, e.g. “If the flame is RED, the ward shatters and the door opens. If the flame is BLUE, the ward holds and the door stays sealed.” Both rule branches specify their endings so that the DSL can derive expected outcomes directly.

Figures 7 and 8 present complete examples for the orb pair under Rule-only instructions and the sign pair under Rule+end instructions, respectively. Each example includes the audited first frame, case specification, two baseline prompts, compiled VisualScript instruction, and the rule program with its settled state.

Appendix B Judging Protocol and Metric Definitions

Fixed-Choice QA.

For each clip the judge answers two scored questions with fixed choices: (Q1) which ending occurs at the end of the clip, with mandated, forbidden, and unclear as the choices. (Q2) asks whether the forbidden outcome appears anywhere in the clip, with yes and no as the choices. The case program specifies both outcomes. Initial-state and action-onset questions are also recorded but excluded from the primary metrics. Answers outside the choice set or missing answers score as incorrect. Fixed answer choices constrain the output format and make verdicts reproducible. The accuracy of the judge’s visual interpretation is audited against blinded human raters in Appendix C.

Judge Inputs.

The judge receives sampled frames, the shared scene description, the action, and the branch-specific expected outcomes. The hidden value, rule program, and expected outcome of the other instance are excluded from the judge inputs. Reproducing a verdict requires the same clips, sampled frames, questions, judge version, and inference settings. The case program fixes the expected outcomes before video generation.

Independent Validation.

The blind human audits in Appendix C assess clip correctness and pairwise preference independently of system identity. That appendix reports agreement between the human ratings and VLM judgments. The reported metrics are therefore produced by a fixed, versioned judge protocol and are validated against blinded human ratings on the audited subset.

B.1 Metric Definitions

All metrics are percentages. Clip-level metrics cover 100 units. An up arrow indicates that higher is better, and a down arrow indicates that lower is better.

  • •

    EndFollow ↑\uparrow requires the final frames to depict the ending specified for that instance.

  • •

    CntAbsent ↑\uparrow requires the forbidden outcome, defined as the required ending for the other instance, to be absent throughout the clip.

  • •

    Strict ↑\uparrow (primary): EndFollow ∧\wedge CntAbsent. The mandated outcome is the only salient ending shown (no contradictory outcome, no both-branch montage).

  • •

    Unclear ↓\downarrow: output unjudgeable (degenerate render, no discernible event). This is counted separately and never credited.

Pair-level metrics (over 50 pairs):

  • •

    PairFollow (twin-joint): both twins individually EndFollow-correct.

  • •

    PairStrict (twin-strict, headline): both twins individually Strict-correct (twin-joint scoring, §4).

  • •

    TwinContrast ↑\uparrow indicates that the judged endings differ between instances A and B. This indicates that the pair is distinguishable and helps diagnose copy-paste behavior.

Probe-contrast metric: Δ\DeltaStrict == Strict(Rule+end) −- Strict(Rule-only). This measures the effect of dictating the ending in addition to the rule instruction. Derived diagnostics (analysis only, Appendix D): the failure triad {direction error (wrong branch taken), leakage-only (right direction but forbidden content also shown), double error}. Branch gap == ||strictA−{}_{A}-strictB|{}_{B}|.

Appendix C Human Audit Platform and Protocols

We assess agreement between the VLM judge and human raters through audits conducted on a web platform (Appendix B). Each auditor receives a numeric identifier and a fixed assignment of evaluation items. The interface displays rendered clips and rule text while concealing system identities, prompts, and instruction conditions. The positions of systems in pairwise comparisons are randomized. The platform operates in two modes, mirroring the two question types of the benchmark.

Clip Verification.

Seventeen cases, comprising nine Rule-only cases and eight Rule+end cases, are evaluated for both hidden states using the full harness, the frozen MiniMax-H3 baseline, and Wan2.2. This produces 102 clips for verification. For each clip, auditors answer the same two fixed choice questions used by the VLM judge. Q1 assesses whether the required ending occurs, and Q2 assesses whether the forbidden outcome appears anywhere in the clip. Both questions include an explicit “unclear” option in the human interface. Each clip receives three independent blinded ratings. Figure 9 shows the clip-verification interface.

Battle Preference.

Twenty-five further case pairs are held out for pairwise comparison. Each pairwise comparison evaluates the full harness against one of four baselines under Rule-only instructions, namely frozen MiniMax-H3, AlayaWorld, Echo-WM, and Wan2.2. The four clips, covering hidden states A and B for each system, play simultaneously in a grid at 2×\times speed. Each comparison receives two independent ratings through a forced choice between the left and right systems, without a tie option. Figure 10 shows the battle grid.

Judge Validation.

Under the same blind evaluation protocol, the VLM judge agrees with the human majority on 91.2 % of the 102 verification clips for Q1 and 86.3 % for Q2. Both rates approach the human reference agreement of 90.2 % and 80.7 %, respectively. The corresponding agreement coefficient is κ=0.72/0.72\kappa=0.72/0.72. System scores show strong rank correlation with human scores on Strict (Spearman ρ=0.94\rho=0.94) and CntAbsent (ρ=1.00\rho=1.00).

Battle Results.

Table 3 reports the human win rate of our full harness per opponent under forced choice. The harness is preferred in 98 % of comparisons, with rates ranging from 96 % to 100 % across baselines. No comparison favors a baseline under the aggregate decision rule, and the remaining comparisons have split auditor votes. At the individual vote level, 99.0 % of votes favor the harness, and agreement between auditor pairs ranges from 95 % to 100 %.

Appendix D Additional Results

The Full Both-Probe Grid.

Table 4 reports every metric under both instruction probes for all eleven backends, followed by the deployed harness condition. The harness is reported as a single condition: its compiler derives the rule branch and the required ending from the case program, so the compiled instruction is the same regardless of probe wording. Table 1 selects one probe per track from this grid. The grid also yields Δ\DeltaStrict, the difference between Rule+end and Rule-only Strict. Pair-level comparisons in §5.2 use exact McNemar tests over the discordant pair counts and paired bootstrap resampling (10 000 resamples) with percentile 95% intervals, taking the pair as the sampling unit. Appendix E provides additional rendered examples under both instruction conditions. Appendix A contains complete prompt examples.

The three instruction conditions form a component chain on WorldState-Bench. Rule-only prompting leaves 32% of pairs jointly correct (Table 1, Track A). Supplying the required ending—a component that the harness’s compiled instruction always includes—raises this to 64% (Table 4). The full harness, which adds deterministic compilation, rule settlement, and the anchored reference channels, reaches 92% with the same frozen weights (§5.2). The increments attribute the gain to outcome specification (+32 points) and to executed state with compiled references (+28 points). Both are significant under the paired exact McNemar test described above (p=4.0×10−4p=4.0\times 10^{-4} and p=2.6×10−3p=2.6\times 10^{-3}), with paired bootstrap 95% CIs of [16,48][16,48] and [12,44][12,44] points. The external channel ablation mirrors the endpoints without our case grammar (Table 8: 74.2 raw text vs. 77.9 full harness overall).
